newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary fin. minister warns of softening 97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Hungary fin. minister warns of softening 97 budget.

text.p: Hungarian Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy said on Saturday that the country needed a strict 1997 budget and he was not satisfied with the pace of the social security reforms.
"If we 'soften', we will need a supplementary budget in 1997, which could have the worst message ahead of elections," he told the daily Nepszabadsag.
"I am not satisfied with the pace of progress in reforms, mainly those concerning the health care system," he said.
The ministry expects Hungary's social security deficit to run as high as 53 billion forints ($335.4 million) this year, compared with a target of 17.8 billion forints.

The draft 1997 budget, which is to be submitted to Parliament on Monday, would widen the field of revenues upon which social security contributions are paid, and slash the spending of state agencies and local municipalities.
Medgyessy said Hungary's economic stabilisation programme, which began in March 1995, should continue to lay the foundations of sustainable growth.
He hoped that the first modest benefits of the stabilisation course would be felt by Hungarians already next year.

The stabilisation programme, aimed at reining in Hungary's soaring budget and current account deficits, caused real wages to slump by some 10 percent in 1995, and Medgyessy acknowledged they could drop by further four to five percent this year, compared with the two percent government target.

Medgyessy said Hungary will keep the system of pre-announced crawling peg forint devaluations next year, but it has not been decided yet whether the current monthly 1.2 percent rate could be reduced next year.
Hungary expects inflation to drop to 18 percent next year from the forecast of 22 to 24 percent for this year.

The minister said Hungary will continue to abolish its seven percent customs surcharge next year, taking import figures and competitiveness into account when deciding about the pace of abolishing the surcharge.
